book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)

chapters.file: ch20 - Colbert Is (the Tragedy and Comedy of) America, and So Are We.md
chapters.relation: Ralkowski asks whether Colbert is America's Socrates, comparing Colbert's ironic interviews (Caitlin Flanagan on feminism, Harvey Mansfield on manliness, Howard Dean's superdelegates, the ABC Stephanopoulos-Gibson debate) to Socrates' definitional refutations of Euthyphro and the Athenian elite. Like Socrates in Plato's cave allegory, Colbert is a shadow on the wall undermining truthiness from within, yet both fail: audiences laugh, guests collect the campaign-donation 'Colbert Bump,' and nothing changes, making America the self-satisfied one who is ignorant of its ignorance. Through Nehamas's contrast of Socratic and Platonic irony and the Symposium's demand that the greatest work read as both tragedy and comedy, the chapter concludes Colbert may be America's Plato — condemning and laughing at us like a Sisyphean liberator who knows we will not leave the cave.

Stone builds a theory of humor from Wittgenstein's philosophy of language: Colbert's Starbucks-withdrawal 'ThreatDown' skit, the peg-leg-pirate quip at the Constitution Center, and the flip from '68% disapprove of the job he's doing' to '68% approve of the job he's not doing' all work as aspect-change (seeing-as), making us see an ordinary scene under a new aspect. Getting the joke requires a shared form of life (recognizing the Starbucks logo, knowing the Danish-cartoon controversy that made Colbert's suspiciously flattering entry on Islam the punchline) plus a personal Humorous Attitude and an avowal — laughter, or the Washington press corps' respectful silence at the 2006 Correspondents' Dinner, which Colbert converted into a second aspect-change for the larger TV and blog audience.

Frazier reads the show through Freud: Stephen play-acts both the repressed religious-right superego (Dobson, Hagee, his terror of bug sex) and the aggressive American id, so his improvised irony — shielding his crotch from Michael Stipe, mangling Teddy Roosevelt's big-stick maxim for Joe Sestak, sneering at the women's-softball sportsmanship story — works as therapeutic catharsis that lets viewers laugh at and tame their own aggression and hang-ups. Against MacIntyre's charge that irony corrodes culture, he enlists Kierkegaard's picture of the ironist who outdoes a view's 'ludicrous enthusiasm' (the U.S.A.! chant at Naomi Wolf, the gun-control interview that collapses into a case against itself), concluding that the man who merely played the true patriot was the more authentic American.

chapters.file: ch23 - What Mr. Colbert Has Taught Us (Besides Everything).md
chapters.relation: In full truthiness voice, Michaud explains Colbert's failed 2008 presidential run — the South Carolina Democratic Executive Council's 13-3 vote keeping him off the ballot — as exactly what Nietzsche predicted: the resentful weak, the 'sheep,' hold the super-man down by redefining meekness as strength. He walks through will-to-power as self-overcoming, the lambs-and-birds-of-prey parable from the Genealogy, and Christianity as slave morality, then 'corrects' Nietzsche by relocating slave morality in the liberal media rather than God, ending with Colbert as the man of the future who 'affirms life without resentment.'

chapters.file: ch24 - FINAL SEGMENT - What Stephen Colbert Tells Us about Being America.md
ch25 - Truthiness and the Denial of Responsibility.md
chapters.relation: Schiller finds a calculated tension in Stephen: he claims impossible literal colorblindness ('People tell me I'm white and I believe them') while staging a nationwide search for a new black friend whose only function is to license racially insensitive talk, as in the Rosa Parks 'Overrated' WØRD where he misreads Alan's cursing as agreement. Working through the N-word debate (Kennedy's Intentionalism, Asim's Eradicationism, Chris Rock's double standard) and Michael Eric Dyson on Hurricane Katrina, he argues Stephen claims the rights of linguistic license while shirking its responsibilities, and that truthiness is the same posture writ large — the 'rhetoric of complexity' by which politicians deny responsibility for the problems they refuse to understand.

chapters.file: ch26 - I’m Done But The Editor Expects Some Sort of Fancy Conclusion.md
chapters.relation: Smith dissects Stephen's free-market worship — the market as a God requiring faith, 'the market has spoken' on global warming, supply-side economics, and the plan to run universities as businesses with credit-card-swiper desks and tuition priced by marketability. Against this he deploys Socrates in the Republic: a practice is defined by its aim, so a physician aiming at his own wealth is not practicing medicine badly but moneymaking, and by the same argument a corporatized university whose primary aim is shareholder profit is no longer higher education — privatization alters its nature and so destroys it, while Smith's invisible hand is exposed as the South Park gnomes' missing Step Two and wikiality as supply-side epistemology where facts are supplied by majority vote instead of known.

Patton and Webb unpack Colbert's coinage 'freem' — freedom without the do — from the first episode's dedication to 'the heroes' who act patriotically by watching TV, through Bush's post-9/11 call to go shopping, the Wikipedia elephant vandalism, and the WristStrong bracelet as activism indistinguishable from consuming Viacom product. Using Singer's argument that social capital (roads, satellites, infrastructure) makes the 'it's your money' cry hollow, E.O. Wilson's four-Earths arithmetic on unsustainable consumption and greenwashed market 'solutions' to global warming, and Baudrillard's Consumer Society account of news packaged for consumption beside the ads, they ask whether the Colbert Nation's ironic participation resists corporate media or completes it, concluding freem converts even critique into one more purchase.

chapters.file: ch28 - TAKE THE ISHIHARA RACE TEST.md
chapters.relation: A mock color-blindness test: readers check figures to see whether they, like Stephen, suffer 'Colbertian Race Blindness,' an affliction of whites that confuses racial equality with racial indifference. The race-blind view history through that impairment — Civil Rights supposedly proved blacks and whites have 'perfectly identical cultures,' and Dr. King's colorblind society becomes a nation where everyone is one color, white — a gag that dramatizes the book's chapter on race by taking Stephen's 'I don't see race' literally.

chapters.file: ch29 - Citizens of the Colbert Nation.md

holes.name: Aspect-Seeing (seeing-as / aspect-dawning)
holes.what: Wittgenstein's notion (the duck-rabbit) that one and the same object can be seen under different aspects, where what changes is our interpretation rather than the object.
holes.why: Chapter 21 defines humor itself as aspect-change, and the taxonomy has no slug for this central Wittgensteinian idea.

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis: the mind as id, ego and superego, with repression of unconscious desire and catharsis as therapeutic release.
holes.why: Chapter 22's whole reading of Colbert as America's id and the fundamentalist superego, whose irony works as catharsis, is Freudian, and Freud is absent from the taxonomy.

holes.name: Psychoanalysis (id, ego, superego, repression)
holes.what: Freud's structural model of the psyche in which a healthy ego balances primal drives (id) against internalized moral authority (superego), with repression and catharsis governing the balance.
holes.why: Chapter 22 uses id/ego/superego dynamics, repression, and catharsis to explain how Colbert's satire is psychologically therapeutic.

holes.name: Irony (Socratic and Kierkegaardian)
holes.what: Kierkegaard's account of irony as earnestly saying what one does not mean — identifying with a view in order to outdo its enthusiasm and expose its emptiness.
holes.why: Chapter 22 grounds Colbert's method in long quotations from Kierkegaard's The Concept of Irony, for which the taxonomy has no slug.

holes.name: Colorblind Racism (racial colorblindness)
holes.what: The ideology that justice means not seeing race at all, which in practice conflates racial equality with racial indifference and excuses ignoring racial disadvantage.
holes.why: Chapter 25 (with the chapter 28 Ishihara Race Test gag) builds its entire argument on the incoherence of Stephen's claim to be literally race-blind.

holes.name: Linguistic License
holes.what: The permission, grounded in group membership or a personal relationship, to say things about a group that outsiders could not say without giving offense.
holes.why: Chapter 25 needs it to explain the 'black friend' bit, the Rosa Parks WØRD, and the N-word debate over who may say what.
